title: Why do we get déjà vu?

lines.text: Have you ever walked into an unfamiliar room and felt an overwhelming certainty you've been there before?
That eerie feeling is called déjà vu, and it is actually a temporary brain glitch.
Normally, incoming sensory information enters your short-term memory before being cataloged into long-term storage.
lines.caps: Normally sensory data goes to *short-term | memory *first

lines.text: During déjà vu, a tiny neurological misfire routes the current experience straight into your long-term memory circuit.
lines.caps: A misfire routes *current sight | straight into *long-term memory!

lines.text: Your temporal lobe perceives a brand new moment as if it occurred years in the past.
lines.caps: Your brain thinks a *new moment | is an ancient *memory

lines.text: It is essentially your brain's memory filing system lagging by a fraction of a millisecond.
lines.caps: Your brain's memory *buffer | lagged for a *millisecond

lines.text: Don't worry; experiencing déjà vu just means your brain's fact-checking system is healthy and active.
